questions.q: The mean free path of molecules in an ideal gas A is half that of another ideal gas B. The diameter of the spherical molecules of gas A is twice the diameter of the molecules of B. If number densities of the gases A and B are $n_A$ and $n_B$, respectively, then the correct option is :
questions.solution:
The mean free path of a gas molecule is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$

Given $\lambda_A = \dfrac{1}{2}\lambda_B$ and $d_A = 2d_B$

Substituting the formula for mean free path:

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d_A^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d_B^2 n_B} \right)$

$\dfrac{1}{d_A^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2 d_B^2 n_B}$

Substituting $d_A = 2d_B$:

$\dfrac{1}{(2d_B)^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2 d_B^2 n_B}$

$\dfrac{1}{4 d_B^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2 d_B^2 n_B}$

$4 n_A = 2 n_B$

$n_A = \dfrac{1}{2} n_B$

Answer: $n_A=\dfrac{1}{2}n_B$

questions.q: An ideal gas is made of polyatomic molecules. Each of the molecules has three translational, three rotational and $f$ number of vibrational modes. If the ratio of heat capacities $C_P/C_V$ of the gas is $8/7$, then the value of $f$ is :
questions.solution:
The internal energy of one mole of the polyatomic gas is given by the equipartition theorem. Each translational and rotational degree of freedom contributes $\dfrac{1}{2}RT$ to the internal energy, while each vibrational mode contributes $RT$ (since it has both kinetic and potential energy components).

$U = 3 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}RT\right) + 3 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}RT\right) + f(RT) = (3+f)RT$

The molar heat capacity at constant volume is:

$C_V = \dfrac{dU}{dT} = (3+f)R$

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is:

$C_P = C_V + R = (4+f)R$

The ratio of heat capacities is given as $\dfrac{8}{7}$:

$\dfrac{C_P}{C_V} = \dfrac{4+f}{3+f} = \dfrac{8}{7}$

$28 + 7f = 24 + 8f$

$f = 4$

Answer: $4$

questions.q:
A flask contains argon and chlorine in the ratio of $2:1$ by mass. The temperature of the mixture is $27^\circ$C. The ratio of root mean square speed of the molecules of the two gases $\left(\dfrac{v_{rms}^{Ar}}{v_{rms}^{Cl}}\right)$ is :
(Atomic mass of argon $= 40.0$ u and molecular mass of chlorine $= 70.0$ u)
questions.solution:
The root mean square speed of a gas molecule is given by $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature and $M$ is the molar mass.

For argon and chlorine in the same flask, the temperature $T$ is the same.

Therefore, the ratio of their rms speeds is inversely proportional to the square root of their molar masses:

$\dfrac{v_{rms}^{Ar}}{v_{rms}^{Cl}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_{Cl}}{M_{Ar}}}$

Given the molecular mass of chlorine $M_{Cl} = 70.0$ u and atomic mass of argon $M_{Ar} = 40.0$ u:

$\dfrac{v_{rms}^{Ar}}{v_{rms}^{Cl}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{70.0}{40.0}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}$

The mass ratio of the gases in the mixture is extra information and not required for this calculation.

Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List I with List II:

  List I   List II
(A) 3 Translational degrees of freedom (I) Monoatomic gases
(B) 3 Translational, 2 rotational degrees of freedoms (II) Polyatomic gases
(C) 3 Translational, 2 rotational and 1 vibrational degrees of freedom (III) Rigid diatomic gases
(D) 3 Translational, 3 rotational and more than one vibrational degrees of freedom (IV) Nonrigid diatomic gases

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The formula for degree of freedom is given by 

f=3N-k

where N is the number of particles, k is the individual relationship in the system.

For a monoatomic gas particle, N=1, k=0. So, f=3

Hence, monoatomic gas has 3 translational degree of freedom.

For a rigid diatomic gas molecule, there are 5 degrees of freedom, 3 translational and 2 rotational. A diatomic gas can have two extra degrees of freedom due to rotation along two independent axes.

A non rigid diatomic molecule has one extra degree of freedom than a rigid one. This is the vibrational degree of freedom. Hence, it has 6 degrees of freedom.

So, a non rigid diatomic gas has 3 translational, 2 rotational and 1 vibrational degrees of freedom.

A polyatomic gas has more than two atoms per molecule. Hence, the total number of degrees of freedom is 3 translational,  3 rotational and more than one vibrational degree of freedom.

\(\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|}
\hline
& \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline
(a) & \text{Root mean square speed}

(b) & \text{Mean free path}

2. (b) Mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels before colliding, and it is given by \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi d^2 n}}\), where \(d\) is the diameter of the molecules, and \(n\) is the number density.
3. (c) Ideal gas equation is represented by the familiar equation \(P V=n R T\), which relates pressure, volume, and temperature of an ideal gas.
4. (d) Degrees of freedom of a diatomic gas is typically 5, accounting for 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom at normal temperatures.
5. (e) Pressure of an ideal gas is related to the root mean square speed by \(P=\frac{1}{3} \rho v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\), where \(\rho\) is the density of the gas.

4. (d) Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution explains the distribution of molecular speeds in a gas and predicts how many molecules have a particular speed at a given temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a linear polyatomic gas having $f$ active vibrational modes. If $\gamma$ is the ratio of specific heat capacities $\left(\dfrac{C_p}{C_v}\right)$ for this gas, the correct expression for the number of vibrational modes $f$ in terms of $\gamma$ is:
questions.solution:
For a linear polyatomic gas, there are 3 translational degrees of freedom and 2 rotational degrees of freedom.

Let the number of active vibrational modes be $f$. Each vibrational mode contributes $R$ to the molar heat capacity at constant volume ($C_v$).

The total $C_v$ is given by:
$C_v = \dfrac{3}{2}R + \dfrac{2}{2}R + fR = \dfrac{5}{2}R + fR = \left(\dfrac{5 + 2f}{2}\right)R$

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure ($C_p$) is:
$C_p = C_v + R = \left(\dfrac{5 + 2f}{2}\right)R + R = \left(\dfrac{7 + 2f}{2}\right)R$

The ratio of specific heats $\gamma$ is:
$\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v} = \dfrac{7 + 2f}{5 + 2f}$

Rearranging to solve for $f$:
$\gamma(5 + 2f) = 7 + 2f$
$5\gamma + 2f\gamma = 7 + 2f$
$2f(\gamma - 1) = 7 - 5\gamma$
$f = \dfrac{7 - 5\gamma}{2(\gamma - 1)}$

Using the formula for a non-linear polyatomic gas would incorrectly yield $\dfrac{4 - 3\gamma}{\gamma - 1}$, and forgetting the factor of 2 in the denominator during algebraic isolation leads to $\dfrac{7 - 5\gamma}{\gamma - 1}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{7 - 5\gamma}{2(\gamma - 1)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The pressure ($P$) versus temperature ($T$ in Kelvin) graph for a fixed mass of an ideal gas shows two straight lines passing through the origin, corresponding to two different constant volumes $V_1$ and $V_2$. The line for $V_1$ is steeper than the line for $V_2$. Two states of the gas, $A$ and $B$, are marked on the lines for $V_1$ and $V_2$ respectively, such that both states have the exact same pressure $P_0$. If $v_A$ and $v_B$ are the root mean square (rms) speeds of the gas molecules in states $A$ and $B$ respectively, which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT \Rightarrow P = \left(\dfrac{nR}{V}\right)T$.

For a $P-T$ graph, the slope is $\dfrac{nR}{V}$. Since the line for $V_1$ is steeper than the line for $V_2$, its slope is greater, which means $V_1 \lt V_2$.

States $A$ and $B$ are at the same pressure $P_0$. From the graph equation $T = \dfrac{PV}{nR}$, at a constant pressure $P_0$, the temperature is directly proportional to the volume. Since $V_1 \lt V_2$, the temperature of state $A$ (on $V_1$) is less than the temperature of state $B$ (on $V_2$), so $T_A \lt T_B$.

The rms speed of gas molecules is given by $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$. Since $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$ and $T_A \lt T_B$, it follows that $v_A \lt v_B$.

Answer: $v_A \lt v_B$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is confined in a container. The initial mean free path of the gas molecules is $\lambda$. If half the mass of the gas is allowed to escape and the volume of the container is simultaneously doubled, what will be the new mean free path of the gas molecules?
questions.solution:
The mean free path ($\lambda$) of gas molecules is given by:
$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$
where $n$ is the number density of the gas molecules.

The number density is defined as the number of molecules per unit volume, $n = \dfrac{N}{V}$.

When half the mass of the gas escapes, the new number of molecules becomes $N' = \dfrac{N}{2}$.
When the volume of the container is doubled, the new volume becomes $V' = 2V$.

The new number density is:
$n' = \dfrac{N'}{V'} = \dfrac{\dfrac{N}{2}}{2V} = \dfrac{N}{4V} = \dfrac{n}{4}$

Since the mean free path is inversely proportional to the number density ($\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{n}$), the new mean free path will be:
$\lambda' = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 \left(\dfrac{n}{4}\right)} = 4 \lambda$

Answer: $4\lambda$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A non-linear polyatomic gas is heated to a temperature such that exactly two of its vibrational modes become active. According to the law of equipartition of energy, the ratio of specific heat capacities $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v}$ for this gas is:
questions.solution:
For a non-linear polyatomic gas, the number of translational degrees of freedom is 3 and the number of rotational degrees of freedom is 3.

According to the law of equipartition of energy, each translational and rotational degree of freedom contributes $\dfrac{1}{2}R$ to the molar heat capacity at constant volume ($C_v$). Each active vibrational mode contributes $R$ to $C_v$ (since it has both kinetic and potential energy components).

Given that there are 2 active vibrational modes:
$C_v = \dfrac{3}{2}R + \dfrac{3}{2}R + 2(R) = 3R + 2R = 5R$

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure ($C_p$) is:
$C_p = C_v + R = 5R + R = 6R$

The ratio of specific heats $\gamma$ is:
$\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v} = \dfrac{6R}{5R} = 1.20$

Assuming a vibrational mode contributes only $\dfrac{1}{2}R$ leads to the incorrect value of 1.25, while ignoring vibrational modes entirely gives 1.33.

Answer: $1.20$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If the temperature of a given mass of gas in a closed rigid vessel is increased, its mean free path remains constant.

Reason (R): The mean free path of a gas is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature at constant volume.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
The mean free path of gas molecules is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$, where $n$ is the number density ($n = \dfrac{N}{V}$).

In a closed rigid vessel, both the total number of molecules ($N$) and the volume ($V$) remain constant. Therefore, the number density ($n$) is constant.

Since $\lambda$ depends only on the molecular diameter and number density, it remains constant even if the temperature is increased. Thus, Assertion (A) is correct.

Reason (R) is incorrect because the mean free path is independent of temperature as long as the volume (and thus number density) is constant.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car tyre contains air at a gauge pressure of $2 \text{ atm}$ and a temperature of $300 \text{ K}$. More air is pumped into the tyre, increasing its total mass by $20\%$. After pumping and driving, the temperature of the air inside the tyre rises to $330 \text{ K}$. Assuming the volume of the tyre remains strictly constant and the atmospheric pressure is $1 \text{ atm}$, what is the final gauge pressure of the air in the tyre?
questions.solution:
The initial absolute pressure of the air in the tyre is $P_1 = P_{\text{gauge}} + P_{\text{atm}} = 2 + 1 = 3 \text{ atm}$.

From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, the absolute pressure is directly proportional to the product of the number of moles and the absolute temperature for a constant volume ($P \propto nT$).

Since the mass of the air increases by $20\%$, the new number of moles is $n_2 = 1.2 n_1$. The initial temperature is $T_1 = 300 \text{ K}$ and the final temperature is $T_2 = 330 \text{ K}$.

The final absolute pressure $P_2$ is given by:
$P_2 = P_1 \times \left(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)$
$P_2 = 3 \times 1.2 \times \left(\dfrac{330}{300}\right) = 3 \times 1.2 \times 1.1 = 3.96 \text{ atm}$.

The final gauge pressure is $P_{2,\text{gauge}} = P_2 - P_{\text{atm}} = 3.96 - 1 = 2.96 \text{ atm}$.

Answer: $2.96 \text{ atm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two ideal gases, helium and oxygen, are maintained in separate containers at identical temperature and pressure. The ratio of the mass density of helium to that of oxygen is:
questions.solution:
The ideal gas equation in terms of mass density $\rho$ is given by $P = \dfrac{\rho RT}{M_0}$, where $M_0$ is the molar mass of the gas.

Rearranging for density, we get $\rho = \dfrac{P M_0}{RT}$.

Since the pressure $P$ and temperature $T$ are identical for both gases, the mass density is directly proportional to the molar mass ($\rho \propto M_0$).

The molar mass of monatomic helium ($He$) is $4$ g/mol and the molar mass of diatomic oxygen ($O_2$) is $32$ g/mol.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{\rho_{He}}{\rho_{O_2}} = \dfrac{4}{32} = \dfrac{1}{8}$, which is $1 : 8$.

Using the atomic mass of oxygen ($16$ g/mol) instead of its molecular mass leads to the incorrect ratio $1 : 4$.

Answer: $1 : 8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two different ideal gases, X and Y, are kept in separate identical flasks at the exact same temperature and pressure. If the mean free path of the molecules of gas X is $9$ times that of gas Y, what is the ratio of the molecular diameters of gas X to gas Y?
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas, the number density $n$ is given by $n = \dfrac{P}{k_B T}$.

Since both gases are at the same pressure and temperature, their number densities are equal ($n_X = n_Y$).

The mean free path is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$.

Since $n$ is constant across both flasks, $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y} = \left(\dfrac{d_Y}{d_X}\right)^2$

Given $\lambda_X = 9\lambda_Y$, we have:

$9 = \left(\dfrac{d_Y}{d_X}\right)^2$

$\dfrac{d_Y}{d_X} = 3$

$\dfrac{d_X}{d_Y} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

The ratio of their molecular diameters is $1:3$.

Answer: $1:3$

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the missing term '$x$' in various forms of the ideal gas equation.

List-IList-II
(A) $P = x \dfrac{RT}{M_0}$(I) Number density
(B) $P = x k_B T$(II) Mass density
(C) $PV = x RT$(III) Molar mass
(D) $PV = \left(\dfrac{m}{x}\right)RT$(IV) Number of moles

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The ideal gas equation can be expressed in various forms.

In the macroscopic form involving mass density $\rho$, the equation is $P = \rho \dfrac{RT}{M_0}$. Thus, in (A), $x$ represents mass density (II).

In the microscopic form, the equation is $P = n_v k_B T$, where $n_v$ is the number density (number of molecules per unit volume). Thus, in (B), $x$ represents number density (I).

The standard molar form is $PV = nRT$, where $n$ is the number of moles. Thus, in (C), $x$ represents the number of moles (IV).

The number of moles $n$ can be written as the ratio of total mass $m$ to molar mass $M_0$, giving $PV = \left(\dfrac{m}{M_0}\right)RT$. Thus, in (D), $x$ represents molar mass (III).

The correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rigid container is initially filled with oxygen gas. A student plots a pressure-temperature ($P-T$) graph for the gas. The initial state of the gas is represented by point A at coordinates $(T_0, P_0)$. After some gas is allowed to leak out, the container is resealed and the gas reaches a new state represented by point B at coordinates $(2T_0, 1.2P_0)$. What percentage of the initial mass of the gas was released from the container?
questions.solution:
From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT \Rightarrow n = \dfrac{PV}{RT}$.

For the initial state A, the number of moles is $n_A = \dfrac{P_0 V}{R T_0}$.

For the final state B, the number of moles is $n_B = \dfrac{1.2 P_0 V}{R (2T_0)} = 0.6 \left(\dfrac{P_0 V}{R T_0}\right) = 0.6 n_A$.

Since the mass of the gas is directly proportional to the number of moles, the remaining mass in the container is $60\%$ of the initial mass.

Therefore, the percentage of the initial mass that leaked out is $100\% - 60\% = 40\%$.

Answer: $40\%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A graph displays straight lines passing through the origin, representing the Volume ($V$) versus Mass ($m$) at STP for four different gases: $\text{O}_2$, $\text{N}_2$, $\text{He}$, and $\text{H}_2$. It is assumed that the intermolecular forces in all these gases vanish completely. The lines are labeled 1, 2, 3, and 4 in decreasing order of their slopes (i.e., line 1 is the steepest). Which of the following correctly identifies the gases corresponding to lines 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively?
questions.solution:
According to the ideal gas equation, the volume $V$ of a gas of mass $m$ and molar mass $M$ at STP is given by:

$V = \dfrac{m}{M} \times 22.4\text{ L}$

The slope of the $V$ versus $m$ graph is $\dfrac{V}{m} = \dfrac{22.4}{M}$.

Thus, the slope is inversely proportional to the molar mass $M$. The gas with the smallest molar mass will have the steepest slope (line 1).

The molar masses of the given gases are:
$\text{H}_2 = 2\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$\text{He} = 4\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$\text{N}_2 = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$\text{O}_2 = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Since $M_{\text{H}_2} \lt M_{\text{He}} \lt M_{\text{N}_2} \lt M_{\text{O}_2}$, the order of decreasing slopes is $\text{H}_2 \gt \text{He} \gt \text{N}_2 \gt \text{O}_2$. Therefore, lines 1, 2, 3, and 4 correspond to $\text{H}_2$, $\text{He}$, $\text{N}_2$, and $\text{O}_2$ respectively.

Answer: $\text{H}_2$, $\text{He}$, $\text{N}_2$, $\text{O}_2$

questions.q:
Match the types of gases in List-I with their corresponding theoretical values of the ratio of specific heats $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v}$ in List-II.

(A) Monoatomic gas(I) $\dfrac{5}{3}$
(B) Diatomic gas (rigid rotor)(II) $\dfrac{7}{5}$
(C) Diatomic gas (with 1 active vibrational mode)(III) $\dfrac{9}{7}$
(D) Non-linear polyatomic gas (rigid, no vibrational mode)(IV) $\dfrac{4}{3}$


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The ratio of specific heats is given by $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v} = 1 + \dfrac{R}{C_v}$.

(A) Monoatomic gas: Has 3 translational degrees of freedom. $C_v = \dfrac{3}{2}R$.
$\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{5}{3}$.

(B) Diatomic gas (rigid rotor): Has 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom. $C_v = \dfrac{5}{2}R$.
$\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{7}{5}$.

(C) Diatomic gas (with 1 active vibrational mode): Has 3 translational, 2 rotational, and 1 vibrational mode. The vibrational mode contributes $R$ to $C_v$.
$C_v = \dfrac{5}{2}R + R = \dfrac{7}{2}R$.
$\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{7} = \dfrac{9}{7}$.

(D) Non-linear polyatomic gas (rigid): Has 3 translational and 3 rotational degrees of freedom. $C_v = \dfrac{6}{2}R = 3R$.
$\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Read the following statements regarding the graphical representation of a given mass of an ideal gas:

(I) In a $V$-$T$ graph (where $V$ is on the y-axis and $T$ is on the x-axis), an isobar with a steeper slope corresponds to a lower pressure.
(II) In a $P$-$T$ graph (where $P$ is on the y-axis and $T$ is on the x-axis), an isochore with a steeper slope corresponds to a higher volume.
(III) In a $P$-$V$ graph, an isotherm further from the origin corresponds to a higher temperature.
(IV) The graph of $PV$ versus $P$ at a constant temperature is a straight line passing through the origin.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct: From the ideal gas equation $V = \left(\dfrac{nR}{P}\right)T$, the slope of a $V$-$T$ graph is $\dfrac{nR}{P}$. A steeper slope means a larger value of $\dfrac{nR}{P}$, which corresponds to a lower pressure.

Statement II is incorrect: From $P = \left(\dfrac{nR}{V}\right)T$, the slope of a $P$-$T$ graph is $\dfrac{nR}{V}$. A steeper slope means a larger value of $\dfrac{nR}{V}$, which corresponds to a lower volume, not higher.

Statement III is correct: In a $P$-$V$ graph, $PV = nRT$. For a higher temperature $T$, the product $PV$ is larger, so the rectangular hyperbola lies further from the origin.

Statement IV is incorrect: At constant temperature, Boyle's law states that $PV = \text{constant}$. Thus, the graph of $PV$ versus $P$ is a horizontal straight line parallel to the pressure axis, not passing through the origin.

Therefore, exactly two statements (I and III) are correct.

Answer: Only two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas has an initial mean free path $\lambda$. If the absolute temperature of the gas is doubled and its pressure is halved, what will be the new mean free path of the gas molecules?
questions.solution:
The mean free path $\lambda$ of a gas molecule is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$

From the ideal gas equation, $P = nkT \implies n = \dfrac{P}{kT}$

Substituting $n$ into the mean free path formula gives:

$\lambda = \dfrac{kT}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$

This shows that for a given gas, the mean free path is directly proportional to the absolute temperature and inversely proportional to the pressure:

$\lambda \propto \dfrac{T}{P}$

When the temperature is doubled ($T' = 2T$) and the pressure is halved ($P' = \dfrac{P}{2}$), the new mean free path $\lambda'$ becomes:

$\lambda' \propto \dfrac{2T}{\dfrac{P}{2}} = 4\left(\dfrac{T}{P}\right)$

Therefore, the new mean free path is $4\lambda$.

Answer: $4\lambda$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $-73\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$, the root mean square (rms) speed of Helium gas molecules is $v$. At what temperature will the rms speed of Hydrogen gas molecules be $100\%$ more than $v$?
questions.solution:
The rms speed of a gas is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$.

For Helium ($M_{\text{He}} = 4\ \text{g/mol}$):
Initial temperature, $T_{\text{He}} = -73 + 273 = 200\ \text{K}$
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{3R(200)}{4}} = \sqrt{150R}$

For Hydrogen ($M_{\text{H}_2} = 2\ \text{g/mol}$):
The target speed is $100\%$ more than $v$, which means the new speed is $v + v = 2v$.
$v_{\text{H}_2} = 2v = 2\sqrt{150R} = \sqrt{4 \times 150R} = \sqrt{600R}$

Equating this to the formula for Hydrogen's rms speed:
$\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT_{\text{H}_2}}{2}} = \sqrt{600R}$

Squaring both sides:
$\dfrac{3T_{\text{H}_2}}{2} = 600$

$T_{\text{H}_2} = \dfrac{600 \times 2}{3} = 400\ \text{K}$

Converting back to Celsius:
$T_{\text{H}_2} = 400 - 273 = 127\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$

Answer: $127\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample of solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) is placed in a chamber. If the intermolecular forces between the molecules were to completely vanish, the substance would occupy a volume of $11.2 \text{ m}^3$ at STP. What is the actual mass of the dry ice sample?
questions.solution:
If the intermolecular forces vanish, the substance behaves as an ideal gas.

The volume occupied by the gas at STP is given as $V = 11.2 \text{ m}^3$.
Since $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1000 \text{ L}$, the volume in liters is:
$V = 11.2 \times 10^3 \text{ L} = 11200 \text{ L}$

The volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at STP is $22.4 \text{ L}$.
Number of moles of $\text{CO}_2$ is:
$n = \dfrac{11200}{22.4} = 500 \text{ mol}$

The molar mass of $\text{CO}_2$ is $44 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
Total mass of the sample is:
$m = n \times M = 500 \times 44 = 22000 \text{ g}$

Converting to kilograms:
$m = 22 \text{ kg}$

Answer: $22 \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding ideal gases is incorrect?
options: At a given temperature and pressure, the number density of all ideal gases is the same.
At a given temperature and pressure, the molar volume of all ideal gases is identical.
At a given temperature and pressure, the mass density of all ideal gases is the same.
At a given temperature and pressure, the mass density of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its molar mass.
questions.solution:
Let us evaluate each statement using the ideal gas equation.

The ideal gas equation is $PV = nRT = N k_B T$.

Number density ($n_v$) is the number of molecules per unit volume: $n_v = \dfrac{N}{V} = \dfrac{P}{k_B T}$. Since it depends only on pressure and temperature, it is the same for all ideal gases at a given $P$ and $T$.

Molar volume is the volume occupied by one mole of gas: $\dfrac{V}{n} = \dfrac{RT}{P}$. This is also identical for all ideal gases at a given $P$ and $T$.

Mass density ($\rho$) is given by $\rho = \dfrac{P M_0}{RT}$, where $M_0$ is the molar mass. Since different gases have different molar masses, their mass densities will be different even at the same temperature and pressure. Thus, the statement claiming mass density is the same for all ideal gases is incorrect.

The formula $\rho = \dfrac{P M_0}{RT}$ also shows that at constant $P$ and $T$, mass density is directly proportional to molar mass.

Answer: At a given temperature and pressure, the mass density of all ideal gases is the same.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A certain amount of a non-linear polyatomic gas having $f$ active vibrational modes undergoes an isobaric expansion. If $Q$ is the heat supplied to the gas and $W$ is the work done by the gas, the ratio $\dfrac{W}{Q}$ is:
questions.solution:
For a non-linear polyatomic gas, the number of translational degrees of freedom is 3 and rotational degrees of freedom is 3.

Each active vibrational mode contributes $R$ to the molar heat capacity at constant volume ($C_v$).

Thus, $C_v = \dfrac{3}{2}R + \dfrac{3}{2}R + fR = (3+f)R$

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is:
$C_p = C_v + R = (4+f)R$

In an isobaric process, the work done by the gas is $W = nR\Delta T$ and the heat supplied is $Q = nC_p\Delta T$.

Therefore, the ratio is:
$\dfrac{W}{Q} = \dfrac{nR\Delta T}{nC_p\Delta T} = \dfrac{R}{C_p} = \dfrac{R}{(4+f)R} = \dfrac{1}{4+f}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4+f}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An ideal gas is maintained at a pressure of $10^5 \text{ N/m}^2$ and a temperature of $300 \text{ K}$. If its mass density is $1.2 \text{ kg/m}^3$, what is the molar mass of the gas?

(Take the universal gas constant $R = \dfrac{25}{3} \text{ J/(mol K)}$)
questions.solution:
The ideal gas equation in terms of mass density $\rho$ is given by:
$P = \dfrac{\rho R T}{M_0}$

Rearranging for molar mass $M_0$:
$M_0 = \dfrac{\rho R T}{P}$

Substitute the given values:
$\rho = 1.2 \text{ kg/m}^3$
$R = \dfrac{25}{3} \text{ J/(mol K)}$
$T = 300 \text{ K}$
$P = 10^5 \text{ N/m}^2$

$M_0 = \dfrac{1.2 \times \left(\dfrac{25}{3}\right) \times 300}{10^5}$
$M_0 = \dfrac{1.2 \times 25 \times 100}{100000}$
$M_0 = \dfrac{3000}{100000} = 0.03 \text{ kg/mol}$

To convert to $\text{g/mol}$, multiply by $1000$:
$M_0 = 0.03 \times 1000 = 30 \text{ g/mol}$.

Answer: $30 \text{ g/mol}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a gas at $27^\circ\text{C}$ is heated such that its rms speed increases by $100\%$, its final temperature must be $1200^\circ\text{C}$.
Reason (R): The rms speed of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the square root of its absolute temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Reason (R) is a correct statement as $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$, which implies $v_{\text{rms}} \propto \sqrt{T}$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature.

For Assertion (A):
Initial temperature, $T_1 = 27^\circ\text{C} = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$.
Let the initial rms speed be $v$. If the speed increases by $100\%$, the final speed $v_2 = v + 100\% \text{ of } v = 2v$.
Since $v_{\text{rms}} \propto \sqrt{T}$, we have $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$.
$\dfrac{2v}{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{300}}$
$4 = \dfrac{T_2}{300} \Rightarrow T_2 = 1200 \text{ K}$.
Converting back to Celsius, final temperature $= 1200 - 273 = 927^\circ\text{C}$.
The assertion claims the final temperature is $1200^\circ\text{C}$, so Assertion (A) is false.

Therefore, (A) is false but (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hypothetical liquid has a molar mass of $22.4 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and a density of $1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$. For any given mass of this substance, what is the ratio of the actual volume it occupies in the liquid state to the volume it would occupy if all intermolecular forces vanished at STP?
questions.solution:
Let us consider $1 \text{ mole}$ of the substance.
The mass of $1 \text{ mole}$ is $22.4 \text{ g}$.

The density of the liquid is $1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, which is equivalent to $1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$ (or $1 \text{ g mL}^{-1}$).
The volume occupied by $1 \text{ mole}$ in the liquid state ($V_{\text{liquid}}$) is:
$V_{\text{liquid}} = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Density}} = \dfrac{22.4 \text{ g}}{1 \text{ g mL}^{-1}} = 22.4 \text{ mL} = 22.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ L}$

If all intermolecular forces vanish, the substance behaves as an ideal gas. The volume occupied by $1 \text{ mole}$ of an ideal gas at STP ($V_{\text{gas}}$) is $22.4 \text{ L}$.

The required ratio is:
$\dfrac{V_{\text{liquid}}}{V_{\text{gas}}} = \dfrac{22.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ L}}{22.4 \text{ L}} = 10^{-3}$

Answer: $10^{-3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The mean free path of gas molecules in a closed rigid container remains unchanged when the temperature of the gas is increased.

Reason (R): The mean free path of gas molecules is inversely proportional to the number density of the gas, which remains constant in a closed rigid container.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
The mean free path of a gas molecule is given by the formula:
$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$
where $d$ is the diameter of the molecule and $n$ is the number density (number of molecules per unit volume, $n = \dfrac{N}{V}$).

In a closed rigid container, both the total number of gas molecules ($N$) and the volume of the container ($V$) remain constant. Therefore, the number density ($n$) of the gas remains constant regardless of any change in temperature.

Since the number density does not change, the mean free path of the gas molecules also remains unchanged. Thus, both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and (R) provides the correct explanation for (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
$20\text{ mL}$ of a liquid substance X (molar mass $= 20\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, density $= 1\text{ g mL}^{-1}$) is sealed in a perfectly rigid container of exactly $20\text{ mL}$ capacity at $273\text{ K}$. If the intermolecular forces between the molecules suddenly vanish, what will be the pressure exerted by the resulting gas on the container walls?

(Assume that $1\text{ mole}$ of an ideal gas occupies $22.4\text{ L}$ at $1\text{ atm}$ and $273\text{ K}$)
questions.solution:
Mass of the liquid substance X $= \text{Volume} \times \text{Density} = 20\text{ mL} \times 1\text{ g mL}^{-1} = 20\text{ g}$.

Number of moles of X, $n = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar mass}} = \dfrac{20\text{ g}}{20\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 1\text{ mol}$.

When intermolecular forces vanish, the substance behaves as an ideal gas. At $273\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$, $1\text{ mole}$ of an ideal gas occupies $22.4\text{ L}$.

The gas is confined to the rigid container of volume $V = 20\text{ mL} = 0.020\text{ L}$.

Using Boyle's Law (since temperature and number of moles are constant):
$P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$
$1\text{ atm} \times 22.4\text{ L} = P_2 \times 0.020\text{ L}$

$P_2 = \dfrac{22.4}{0.020} = 1120\text{ atm}$.

Answer: $1120\text{ atm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is subjected to a thermodynamic process in which its absolute temperature is doubled and its pressure is quadrupled. If the initial mean free path of the gas molecules is $\lambda_0$, what is the final mean free path of the molecules?
questions.solution:
The mean free path of a gas molecule is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$

From the ideal gas equation, $P = n k_B T$, the number density $n$ can be written as $n = \dfrac{P}{k_B T}$.

Substituting this into the mean free path formula gives:

$\lambda = \dfrac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$

This shows that for a given gas, the mean free path is directly proportional to the absolute temperature and inversely proportional to the pressure:

$\lambda \propto \dfrac{T}{P}$

Given that the final temperature $T_f = 2T_i$ and the final pressure $P_f = 4P_i$, the new mean free path $\lambda_f$ is:

$\lambda_f = \lambda_0 \left( \dfrac{T_f}{T_i} \right) \left( \dfrac{P_i}{P_f} \right)$

$\lambda_f = \lambda_0 \left( 2 \right) \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = \dfrac{\lambda_0}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\lambda_0}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature of an ideal gas is increased from $-173\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $127\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$. What is the percentage increase in the root mean square (rms) speed of the gas molecules?
questions.solution:
The root mean square (rms) speed of gas molecules is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$.

This implies that $v \propto \sqrt{T}$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

Initial temperature, $T_1 = -173 + 273 = 100\ \text{K}$
Final temperature, $T_2 = 127 + 273 = 400\ \text{K}$

Taking the ratio of the final speed to the initial speed:
$\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{400}{100}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$

This means $v_2 = 2v_1$.

The percentage increase in the rms speed is:
$\dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{v_1} \times 100\% = \dfrac{2v_1 - v_1}{v_1} \times 100\% = 100\%$

Answer: $100\%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A rigid container holds Helium gas at an initial temperature of $127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The total translational kinetic energy of the gas is $50 \mathrm{~kJ}$. A valve is opened, allowing some gas to escape, and the remaining gas is cooled to $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the new total translational kinetic energy of the gas is $15 \mathrm{~kJ}$, what is the mass of the Helium gas that escaped?
[Given: $R = \dfrac{25}{3} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ and molar mass of $\mathrm{He} = 4 \mathrm{~g/mol}$]
questions.solution:
The total translational kinetic energy of an ideal gas is given by $E = \dfrac{3}{2}nRT$.

For the initial state ($T_1 = 127^{\circ} \mathrm{C} = 400 \mathrm{~K}$):
$n_1 = \dfrac{2E_1}{3RT_1} = \dfrac{2 \times 50000}{3 \times \left(\dfrac{25}{3}\right) \times 400} = \dfrac{100000}{25 \times 400} = 10 \mathrm{~mol}$

For the final state ($T_2 = 27^{\circ} \mathrm{C} = 300 \mathrm{~K}$):
$n_2 = \dfrac{2E_2}{3RT_2} = \dfrac{2 \times 15000}{3 \times \left(\dfrac{25}{3}\right) \times 300} = \dfrac{30000}{25 \times 300} = 4 \mathrm{~mol}$

Number of moles of Helium that escaped $= n_1 - n_2 = 10 - 4 = 6 \mathrm{~mol}$

Mass of escaped Helium $= \text{moles} \times \text{molar mass} = 6 \mathrm{~mol} \times 4 \mathrm{~g/mol} = 24 \mathrm{~g}$

Answer: $24 \mathrm{~g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Read the following statements carefully:
(A) If the temperature of a gas in $^\circ\text{C}$ is doubled, its rms speed increases by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.
(B) To increase the rms speed of a gas by $50\%$, its absolute temperature must be increased by $125\%$.
(C) At a given temperature, the rms speed of $\text{SO}_2$ gas is half that of $\text{CH}_4$ gas.
(D) If the volume of a given mass of gas is halved at constant temperature, its rms speed is doubled.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is incorrect because the rms speed is proportional to the square root of absolute temperature (in Kelvin), not temperature in $^\circ\text{C}$.

Statement (B) is correct. Let initial speed be $v$ and absolute temperature be $T$. The new speed $v' = v + 0.5v = 1.5v$. Since $v \propto \sqrt{T}$, $T' \propto (v')^2 = (1.5v)^2 = 2.25 v^2$. Thus, $T' = 2.25T$. The percentage increase in temperature is $\dfrac{2.25T - T}{T} \times 100\% = 125\%$.

Statement (C) is correct. $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$. At constant temperature, $v_{\text{rms}} \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$. Molar mass of $\text{SO}_2 = 64 \text{ g/mol}$ and $\text{CH}_4 = 16 \text{ g/mol}$. Ratio $\dfrac{v_{\text{SO}_2}}{v_{\text{CH}_4}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{16}{64}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Statement (D) is incorrect. The rms speed of gas molecules depends only on the absolute temperature and molar mass. It is independent of volume or pressure as long as the temperature is constant.

Therefore, only two statements, (B) and (C), are correct.

Answer: Only two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A graph is plotted between pressure ($P$) on the y-axis and density ($\rho$) on the x-axis for a given mass of an ideal gas. The graph shows three straight lines passing through the origin, corresponding to three different constant temperatures $T_1$, $T_2$, and $T_3$. If the line for $T_1$ is the steepest and the line for $T_3$ is the least steep, which of the following represents the correct relationship between the temperatures?
questions.solution:
From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$. We know that the number of moles $n = \dfrac{m}{M}$ and density $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$.

Substituting these, we get $P = \left(\dfrac{m}{M}\right) \dfrac{RT}{V} \Rightarrow P = \left(\dfrac{RT}{M}\right)\rho$.

For a $P$ versus $\rho$ graph, the equation is of the form $y = mx$, where the slope $m = \dfrac{RT}{M}$.

Thus, the slope of the line is directly proportional to the temperature $T$. Since the line for $T_1$ is the steepest (maximum slope) and $T_3$ is the least steep (minimum slope), it follows that $T_1 \gt T_2 \gt T_3$.

Answer: $T_1 \gt T_2 \gt T_3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Four ideal gases P, Q, R, and S have their molecular diameters and number densities given as follows:

Gas P: diameter = $d_0$, number density = $n_0$
Gas Q: diameter = $2d_0$, number density = $0.5n_0$
Gas R: diameter = $0.5d_0$, number density = $2n_0$
Gas S: diameter = $0.5d_0$, number density = $0.5n_0$

Which of the four gases has the maximum mean free path?
questions.solution:
The mean free path $\lambda$ of a gas molecule is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$

Thus, the mean free path is inversely proportional to the square of the molecular diameter and inversely proportional to the number density ($\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2 n}$).

Let us calculate the relative factor $\dfrac{1}{d^2 n}$ for each gas:

For Gas P: $\dfrac{1}{(1)^2 \times 1} = 1$

For Gas Q: $\dfrac{1}{(2)^2 \times 0.5} = \dfrac{1}{4 \times 0.5} = 0.5$

For Gas R: $\dfrac{1}{(0.5)^2 \times 2} = \dfrac{1}{0.25 \times 2} = 2$

For Gas S: $\dfrac{1}{(0.5)^2 \times 0.5} = \dfrac{1}{0.25 \times 0.5} = 8$

Gas S has the largest relative factor, and therefore it has the maximum mean free path.

Answer: Gas S

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A rigid cylinder of volume $25 \mathrm{~L}$ contains $140 \mathrm{~g}$ of nitrogen gas ($\mathrm{N_2}$) at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. A valve is opened and $56 \mathrm{~g}$ of the gas is allowed to leak out. If the temperature of the cylinder is allowed to return to $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, what is the final gauge pressure of the gas in the cylinder?
[Given: $R = \dfrac{25}{3} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$, $1 \mathrm{~atm} = 10^5 \mathrm{~N/m}^2$, and molar mass of $\mathrm{N_2} = 28 \mathrm{~g/mol}$]
questions.solution:
Initial mass of $\mathrm{N_2}$ gas $= 140 \mathrm{~g}$

Mass of gas leaked $= 56 \mathrm{~g}$

Final mass of gas remaining in the cylinder $= 140 - 56 = 84 \mathrm{~g}$

Number of moles remaining, $n = \dfrac{84}{28} = 3 \mathrm{~mol}$

Using the ideal gas equation for the final state:
$P_{\mathrm{abs}} V = nRT$

$P_{\mathrm{abs}} = \dfrac{nRT}{V} = \dfrac{3 \times \left(\dfrac{25}{3}\right) \times 300}{25 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{25 \times 300}{25 \times 10^{-3}} = 3 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~Pa}$

Since $1 \mathrm{~atm} = 10^5 \mathrm{~Pa}$, the absolute pressure is $3 \mathrm{~atm}$.

Gauge pressure is the pressure in excess of atmospheric pressure:
$P_{\mathrm{gauge}} = P_{\mathrm{abs}} - P_{\mathrm{atm}} = 3 \mathrm{~atm} - 1 \mathrm{~atm} = 2 \mathrm{~atm}$

Answer: $2 \mathrm{~atm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a given mass of an ideal gas, if a graph is plotted between Volume ($V$) on the y-axis and absolute Temperature ($T$) on the x-axis for two different pressures $P_1$ and $P_2$, the line making a smaller angle with the x-axis corresponds to the higher pressure.

Reason (R): According to the ideal gas equation, at constant volume, the pressure of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, we can write $V = \left(\dfrac{nR}{P}\right)T$.

For a $V$-$T$ graph, the slope of the straight line is given by $m = \tan\theta = \dfrac{nR}{P}$.

A smaller angle $\theta$ with the x-axis implies a smaller slope. Since the slope is inversely proportional to the pressure $P$, a smaller slope corresponds to a higher pressure. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R) states that at constant volume, $P \propto T$. This is Gay-Lussac's law, which is a true statement.

However, the correct explanation for Assertion (A) relies on Charles's law (constant pressure process) and the inverse relationship between the slope of the $V$-$T$ graph and pressure, not on the constant volume process described in Reason (R).

Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two ideal gases A and B are maintained at the same temperature and pressure. If the diameter of a molecule of gas A is twice the diameter of a molecule of gas B, what is the ratio of the mean free path of gas A to that of gas B?
questions.solution:
The mean free path $\lambda$ of a gas molecule is given by the formula:

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$

where $d$ is the molecular diameter and $n$ is the number density of molecules.

Since both gases are at the same temperature and pressure, their number density $n$ is the same. Therefore, the mean free path is inversely proportional to the square of the molecular diameter:

$\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$

Given that $d_A = 2d_B$, the ratio of their mean free paths is:

$\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \left(\dfrac{d_B}{d_A}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{d_B}{2d_B}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Hence, the ratio is $1:4$.

Answer: $1:4$

questions.q: If $7 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~N}_2$ is mixed with $20 \mathrm{~g}$ Ar then $C_P / C_V$ of the mixture will be

questions.q:
Assertion : Equal masses of helium and oxygen gases are given equal quantities of heat. The rise in temperature of helium is greater than that in the case of oxygen.
Reason: The molecular mass of oxygen is more than the molecular mass of helium.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion.
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
If assertion is true but reason is false.
If both assertion and reason are false.
questions.solution: Heat given to helium is totally used up in increasing the translation energy of its molecules since it is a monoatomic gas. On the other hand, in case of oxygen, which is a diatomic gas, heat is used up in increasing the translational, rotational and vibrational energies of its molecules. The rise in temperature of a gas is due to only increase in translational energy of its molecules.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $n$ mole of a gas changes its temperature from $T_1$ to $T_2$ at pressure $P$. If $C_P$ is given of the gas what is change in entropy?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathbf{} d Q=n C_P d T \\ & \frac{d Q}{T}=n C_P \frac{d T}{T} ; d S=n C_P \frac{d T}{T} \\ & \Delta S=n C_P \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \frac{d T}{T}=n C_P \ln \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A closed vessel explodes at $15 \mathrm{~atm}$ pressure. If temperature of the vessel is $300 \mathrm{~K}$ at $10 \mathrm{~atm}$ pressure then find at what temperature will vessel explodes
questions.solution:
For a closed vessel,
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{P_1}{T_1}=\frac{P_2}{T_2} \Rightarrow \frac{10}{300}=\frac{15}{T_2} \\ & T_2=450 \mathrm{~K}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : The total translational kinetic energy of all the molecules of a given mass of an ideal gas is 1.5 times the product of its pressure and its volume.
Reason : The molecules of a gas collide with each other and the velocities of the molecules change due to collision.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion.
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
If assertion is true but reason is false.
If both assertion and reason are false.
questions.solution:
Average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule is $E=\frac{3}{2} k T$
For all gas molecules
$E=\frac{3}{2} k T \times N_A=\frac{3}{2} R T=\frac{3}{2} P V$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two chambers containing $m_1 \mathrm{~g}$ and $m_2 \mathrm{~g}$ of a gas at pressures $P_1$ and $P_2$ respectively are put in communication with each other, temperature remaining constant. The common pressure reached will be
questions.solution:
According to Boyle'slaw, $P V=k$ (a constant)
or $P \frac{m}{\rho}=k$ or $\rho=\frac{P m}{k}\left(\because V=\frac{m}{\rho}\right)\rho=\frac{P}{K}\left(\because \frac{k}{m}=K\right.$ a constant $)$
So, $\rho_1=\frac{P_1}{K}$ and $V_1=\frac{m_1}{\rho_1}=\frac{m_1}{P_1 / K}=\frac{K m_1}{P_1}$
Similarly, $V_2=\frac{K m_2}{P_2}\therefore \quad$ Total volume $=V_1+V_2=K\left(\frac{m_1}{P_1}+\frac{m_2}{P_2}\right)$
Let $P$ be the common pressure and $\rho$ be the common density of mixture. Then
$\begin{aligned} & \rho=\frac{m_1+m_2}{V_1+V_2}=\frac{m_1+m_2}{K\left(\frac{m_1}{P_1}+\frac{m_2}{P_2}\right)} \\ \therefore \quad P & =K \rho=\frac{m_1+m_2}{\frac{m_1}{P_1}+\frac{m_2}{P_2}}=\frac{P_1 P_2\left(m_1+m_2\right)}{\left(m_1 P_2+m_2 P_1\right)}\end{aligned}$

When we heat the gas at constant volume, the heat is supplied to raise the temperature of gas only. When we heat the gas at constant pressure, the volume of the gas apart from temperature of the gas rises. When the gas expands, it does some external work for increasing the volume. So in this case, the heat is supplied.
(a) to raise the temperature of the gas.
(b) to do the mechanical work for expansion. As a result more amount of heat is required to increase the temperature of the gas through the same amount when the pressure is kept constant. Hence $C_P$ is always greater than the value of $C_V$.
